summary: A country in Central America bordered by the Caribbean Sea to the north and the Gulf of Fonseca on the Pacific to the south; it has the ancient Maya city ruins of Copán and is known for exporting bananas and coffee.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: In the 19th century the Bay Islands and the Mosquito Coast, under British control, already had Protestant churches such as the Methodists and Baptists, and in the 1930s the Moravian Church also came from Nicaragua to preach among the Miskito. After the 1970s, American Evangelicals and Pentecostals entered Honduras in large numbers, and after Hurricane Mitch of 1998 caused great damage, the relief and reconstruction work of the various Evangelical groups further expanded their influence. Evangelicalism attracts large numbers of followers with small community churches and networks of mutual aid, and has surpassed Catholicism to become the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1502 Columbus on his fourth voyage reached the north coast of Honduras, and it is generally thought that the first Catholic Mass on the American mainland was held here. In the 1520s–30s Spain conquered Honduras, and although it was resisted by the Lenca chief Lempira and others, Catholicism became the mainstream with colonization. The Virgin of Suyapa, discovered in 1747, later became the national patroness, but with the rise of Evangelicalism the proportion of Catholics has fallen quickly over the past thirty years.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are mainly young people in cities such as the capital Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula, related to urbanization, rising education levels and distrust of religious institutions, and have increased markedly in recent years.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: These include Jehovah's Witnesses, Mormons, and traditional beliefs such as the Garifuna "dügü" ancestral ritual that blends ancestor worship with Catholicism; all are very few in number.

religion.background: Honduras originally had indigenous beliefs of the Maya, Lenca and others, and Copán in the west was an important city of the Classic Maya civilization. After the Spanish conquest in the 16th century Catholicism became the state religion, and the Liberal reforms of the 19th century weakened the church's position and instituted separation of church and state. The activities of the British along the Caribbean coast brought Protestantism, and in the late 20th century American Evangelical missionary work, together with natural disasters and internal turmoil, led Protestantism to expand rapidly, so Honduras has become one of the countries in Central America with the highest proportion of Evangelicals.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish conquistadors entered Honduras from 1524, the colonial government ruled in Spanish, and indigenous peoples such as the Lenca gradually switched to Spanish in the course of colonization, making the mixed-race Mestizos the bulk of the population. After independence in 1821 Spanish became the sole official language, and today almost the entire population has it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Garifuna
ranking.description: The Garifuna are the descendants of intermarriage between indigenous Caribs and Africans; they originally lived on the island of Saint Vincent, were exiled by the British to the island of Roatán off Honduras in 1797, and then settled along the Caribbean coast of Central America. The Garifuna language belongs to the Arawakan family and is mixed with Carib, French, English and Spanish vocabulary; in 2001 the Garifuna language, dance and music were proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO.

ranking.name: English (Bay Islands Creole English)
ranking.description: In the early 19th century large numbers of English-descended and African-descended immigrants from places such as the Cayman Islands settled in the Bay Islands, which were under British control for a long time and were returned to Honduras by treaty around 1860. The islanders have therefore used Caribbean English Creole as their everyday language to this day, and the flourishing tourist industry has made English more important there as well.

language.history: Before colonization Honduras had indigenous languages such as Lenca, Ch'orti' Maya, Pech and Miskito, and after the Spanish conquest most were gradually replaced by Spanish, and Lenca has disappeared. At the end of the 18th century the Garifuna were exiled to the Caribbean coast, bringing the Garifuna language, and British influence in the Bay Islands and the Mosquitia left an English Creole. Today Spanish is the nationwide official language, while minority languages such as Miskito and Garifuna continue in coastal areas.

ranking.name: Baleada
ranking.description: A large flour tortilla is heated, spread with refried beans, sprinkled with crumbled hard cheese and sour cream, and folded in half; egg, avocado or meat may be added.
ranking.history: The baleada originated around San Pedro Sula and La Ceiba on the north coast of Honduras, which in the 20th century were plantation areas of American banana companies, where the supply of flour and the needs of workers made this cheap and filling food popular. The name means "shot", and folklore says it was named after a woman who sold the tortillas being hit by a stray bullet, but this is hard to verify. It is Honduras's most representative street snack and can be had for breakfast or as a late-night meal.

ranking.name: Conch soup (sopa de caracol)
ranking.description: A thick soup stewed from conch meat with coconut milk, cassava, green plantain, carrot and spices such as cilantro; the flavor is fresh and sweet with a rich coconut aroma.
ranking.history: Conch soup originates on the Caribbean coast of Honduras and is linked with the Garifuna food tradition of cooking with coconut milk and seafood. In 1991 the song "Sopa de Caracol" (the original was composed by Garifuna musicians), sung by the Honduran band Banda Blanca, swept Latin America and made the soup famous. It is a signature dish at tourist restaurants on the Bay Islands and the north coast.

ranking.name: Nacatamal
ranking.description: A large tamale in which corn dough is filled with pork or chicken, rice, potato, olives and capers, wrapped in plantain leaves and steamed.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Nahuatl "nacatl" (meat) and "tamalli" (wrapped corn dough), showing its indigenous Mesoamerican origin; after colonization pork, rice and olives introduced by the Spanish were added. Because making it requires mobilizing the whole family, Hondurans usually make them in large numbers during Christmas and New Year and distribute them to relatives and friends, and eating one with coffee on a weekend morning is also a habit of many families.

ranking.name: Seafood and coconut stew (tapado)
ranking.description: A thick soup in which seafood such as fish, crab and shrimp is stewed in coconut milk together with green plantain and cassava; the flavor is fresh and sweet with the aroma of spices.
ranking.history: Tapado is a traditional Garifuna dish; after they were exiled by the British to the Caribbean coast of Honduras in 1797, they lived by fishing and growing cassava in coastal villages, so coconut milk, plantain and seafood became the core of their diet. It represents the distinctive cuisine of Afro-Caribbean culture on Honduras's north coast and is an important dish at local community gatherings and for hosting visitors.

ranking.name: Carne asada
ranking.description: Marinated thin slices of beef are grilled over charcoal and eaten with refried beans, fried plantain, tortillas and tomato-and-onion salsa (chismol).
ranking.history: Spanish colonizers brought cattle to Central America in the 16th century, and places such as Olancho in the east later developed large-scale cattle ranching, making beef an important meat for Hondurans. Carne asada is a typical dish at weekend gatherings of family and friends, grilled over an outdoor fire and served with the local tomato-and-onion salsa, showing the tradition of Honduran cattle-ranching culture.
